summary: This chapter covers why commercial drivers inspect their vehicles, what defects to look for, and how to do an inspection the same way every time. Federal and state laws require drivers to inspect their vehicles, and inspectors can put an unsafe vehicle out of service until it is fixed.

There are three kinds of inspection. The pre-trip inspection finds problems before you leave. During the trip, you watch your gauges, use your senses, and check critical items such as tires, brakes, lights, trailer connections, and cargo securement whenever you stop. The after-trip inspection and report tell the motor carrier what needs repair.

The defects to know are specific. Front tires need at least 4/32 inch of tread in every major groove and other tires at least 2/32 inch. Steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees makes steering hard. Rust around wheel nuts may mean they are loose. You must also carry spare fuses (unless the vehicle has circuit breakers), three red reflective triangles, and a charged fire extinguisher.

concepts.definition: A full check of the vehicle before driving, done in the same order every time so nothing is missed. Safety for you and others is the most important reason to do it.
concepts.tip: Same order every time means you do not forget a step.

concepts.definition: Front (steering) tires need at least 4/32 inch of tread in every major groove. All other tires need at least 2/32 inch. No fabric should show through the tread or sidewall.
concepts.tip: Front 4, others 2 (in 32nds of an inch).

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: Free movement of the steering wheel before the wheels turn. More than 10 degrees, about 2 inches at the rim of a 20-inch wheel, can make the vehicle hard to steer.
concepts.tip: 10 degrees is about 2 inches at the rim.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: Spare electrical fuses (unless the vehicle has circuit breakers), three red reflective warning triangles, and a properly charged and rated fire extinguisher.
concepts.tip: Fuses, three triangles, and an extinguisher.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: Pump the brake pedal three times, then press firmly and hold for five seconds. If the pedal moves, there may be a leak or other problem. Get it fixed before driving.
concepts.tip: Pump three, hold five, pedal should not move.

concepts.definition: A vehicle is put out of service if one-fourth or more of the leaves in any spring assembly are broken, if any leaf is missing or separated, or if any main leaf is broken.
concepts.tip: A quarter of the leaves broken is too many.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

points: Safety is the most important reason to inspect your vehicle.
Front tires need at least 4/32 inch of tread. Other tires need at least 2/32 inch.
Recapped, regrooved, or retreaded tires are not allowed on the front wheels of a bus.
Oil pressure should come up to normal within seconds after the engine starts.
At each stop during a trip, check tires, wheels, rims, brakes, lights, trailer connections, and cargo securement.

summary: This chapter covers the basic skills for moving a heavy vehicle under control: starting smoothly, steering firmly, stopping smoothly, backing safely, and shifting gears. These skills matter more in a large vehicle because mistakes take longer to correct.

When you start on a hill with a manual transmission, partly engage the clutch before you take your foot off the brake so you do not roll back. Hold the wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides. Backing is always dangerous, so avoid it when you can. When you must back, do it slowly in the lowest reverse gear, toward the driver's side, and with a helper when possible.

Most heavy manual transmissions need double clutching. Downshift before you start down a hill and before you enter a curve. A retarder helps slow the vehicle and saves the brakes, but it can make the drive wheels skid, so turn it off on wet, icy, or snowy roads.

concepts.definition: Look at your path first, use mirrors on both sides, back slowly in the lowest reverse gear, back toward the driver's side, and use a helper when you can.
concepts.tip: Slow, driver's side, with a helper.

concepts.definition: A helper stands near the back where you can see them and guides you through blind spots. Before backing, agree on hand signals, and above all on the signal for stop.
concepts.tip: The stop signal is the one that prevents crashes.

concepts.definition: A way to shift a manual transmission: clutch in and shift to neutral, release the clutch, match engine speed to the next gear, then clutch in and shift. If you miss a gear, return to neutral, match engine speed to road speed, and try again.
concepts.tip: Never force a missed shift.

concepts.definition: Downshift before starting down a hill so you can control speed without hard braking, and before entering a curve so you can use a little power through it.
concepts.tip: Shift down before the hill and before the curve.

concepts.definition: A device that slows the vehicle and reduces brake wear. It brakes only the drive wheels, so it can make them skid on wet, icy, or snow-covered roads. Turn it off in those conditions.
concepts.tip: Slippery road, retarder off.

points: Hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides.
Back slowly in the lowest reverse gear, toward the driver's side when possible.
Agree on a stop signal with your helper before backing.
Downshift before hills and curves.
Turn off the retarder on wet, icy, or snow-covered roads.

summary: This chapter covers how to see what is happening around a large vehicle and how to let other road users know what you are doing. Not looking properly is a major cause of crashes, and other drivers may not notice even a big truck in plain sight.

Look 12 to 15 seconds ahead, which is about one block in town and about a quarter mile on the highway, and shift your eyes between near and far. Check your mirrors often, and more often during lane changes, turns, merges, and tight moves. Convex mirrors show a wider view, but they make things look smaller and farther away than they are.

Signal early and keep signaling until the turn is done. Flash your brake lights to warn drivers behind you when you will slow down, and do not wave other drivers by. When you stop on a road or shoulder, turn on your flashers and put out warning devices within 10 minutes. On a two-way road, place them within 10 feet of the front or rear corner, 100 feet behind, and 100 feet ahead. On a one-way or divided highway, place them 10, 100, and 200 feet back toward traffic.

concepts.definition: Look 12 to 15 seconds ahead of your vehicle. In town that is about one block, and at highway speed it is about a quarter of a mile.
concepts.tip: 12 to 15 seconds: a block in town, a quarter mile on the highway.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: A curved mirror that shows a wider area than a flat mirror. Everything in it looks smaller and farther away than it really is.
concepts.tip: Closer than it looks.

concepts.definition: When a commercial vehicle stops on the traveled part or shoulder of a highway (other than for traffic), the driver must put out warning devices as soon as possible and within 10 minutes.
concepts.tip: Flashers on at once, triangles out within 10 minutes.

source.org: 49 CFR 392.22 (FMCSA)

concepts.definition: On a two-lane road with traffic both ways, or an undivided highway: one device within 10 feet of the front or rear corner, one 100 feet behind, and one 100 feet ahead.
concepts.tip: Two-way traffic, so warn both ways: 10, 100 behind, 100 ahead.

source.org: 49 CFR 392.22 (FMCSA)

concepts.definition: On a one-way or divided highway: place devices 10 feet, 100 feet, and 200 feet back toward the approaching traffic.
concepts.tip: One-way traffic, so all three go behind: 10, 100, 200.

source.org: 49 CFR 392.22 (FMCSA)

concepts.definition: Do not signal other drivers that it is safe to pass. You could cause a crash, and you could be blamed for it.
concepts.tip: Drive your own vehicle, not theirs.

points: Look 12 to 15 seconds ahead.
Convex mirrors make things look smaller and farther away.
Flash your brake lights to warn drivers behind you before slowing.
Put out warning devices within 10 minutes of stopping.
Two-way road: 10 feet, 100 feet behind, 100 feet ahead. Divided highway: 10, 100, and 200 feet behind.

compare.title: Where to place warning triangles
rows: Within 10 feet of the front or rear corner, 100 feet behind, 100 feet ahead
10 feet, 100 feet, and 200 feet back toward approaching traffic

summary: This chapter covers how speed and space keep a large vehicle out of trouble. Driving too fast is a major cause of fatal crashes, and heavy vehicles need much more room to stop and turn than cars do.

Total stopping distance is perception distance plus reaction distance plus braking distance. When you double your speed, braking distance becomes about four times longer. Wet roads can double stopping distance, so cut your speed by about one-third on a wet road and by half or more on packed snow. If you hydroplane, release the accelerator and push in the clutch, and do not brake. Empty trucks can take longer to stop because they have less traction.

Keep at least one second of following distance for every 10 feet of vehicle length below 40 mph, and add one more second above 40 mph. If someone tailgates you, add space in front and slow down gradually. Watch the space overhead, since an empty van sits higher than a loaded one. On right turns, keep the rear near the curb and turn wide at the end, and with two left-turn lanes, use the outside one.

concepts.definition: Perception distance (until your brain recognizes the hazard) plus reaction distance (until your foot hits the brake) plus braking distance (until the vehicle stops).
concepts.tip: See it, react, brake: three distances add up.

concepts.definition: Braking distance grows much faster than speed. Doubling your speed from 20 to 40 mph makes the braking distance and the force of impact about four times greater.
concepts.tip: Twice the speed, four times the distance.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: Keep at least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length below 40 mph. Above 40 mph, add 1 more second. A 40-foot truck needs 4 seconds below 40 mph and 5 seconds above it.
concepts.tip: Length divided by 10, plus 1 at highway speed.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: On a wet road, slow down by about one-third, for example from 55 to about 35 mph. On packed snow, slow by half or more. On ice, slow to a crawl and stop as soon as you safely can.
concepts.tip: Wet: one-third off. Snow: half off. Ice: crawl.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: Tires ride on a layer of water and lose contact with the road. It can happen as low as 30 mph with a lot of water, and is more likely with low tire pressure or worn tread. Release the accelerator and push in the clutch. Do not brake.
concepts.tip: Like water skiing: ease off and let the wheels roll.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: On a right turn, keep the rear close to the curb and turn wide as you finish, so no one passes on your right. With two left-turn lanes, use the outside (right-hand) one.
concepts.tip: Do not swing left before a right turn.

points: Total stopping distance = perception + reaction + braking distance.
Double the speed and braking distance becomes about four times longer.
Following distance: 1 second per 10 feet of length, plus 1 second above 40 mph.
If you are tailgated, add space in front and slow down gradually.
An empty van is taller than a loaded one, so check bridge clearance again.
Empty trucks can need more distance to stop than loaded trucks.

summary: This chapter covers seeing hazards before they become emergencies, and staying fit and focused enough to react to them. A hazard is any road condition or road user that could become a danger, such as a driver drifting toward an exit, a stopped delivery truck, or children playing near the road.

Move-over laws ask you to slow down and, when safe, change to a lane not next to an emergency vehicle or work zone on the roadside. Distracted drivers drift and change speed, so give them room. If an aggressive driver confronts you, get out of their way, avoid eye contact, and do not respond to gestures. Federal rules ban texting and hand-held phone use while driving a commercial vehicle, except to contact police or emergency services.

It is illegal to drive a commercial vehicle with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04% or more, and any detectable alcohol below that puts you out of service for 24 hours. Only time sobers a person up. Fatigue is just as dangerous: when you are drowsy, the only real cure is to get off the road and sleep, and a short nap does more than a coffee stop.

concepts.definition: Any road condition or other road user (driver, bicyclist, pedestrian) that could become a danger. Seeing it early gives you time to plan a way out.
concepts.tip: A hazard is a possible emergency. Spot it early.

concepts.definition: When you approach an emergency vehicle stopped on the roadside or a work zone, slow down and move to a lane not next to it if it is safe. If you cannot change lanes, slow down and pass with caution.
concepts.tip: Lights on the shoulder: slow down and move over.

concepts.definition: Federal rules ban texting and using a hand-held mobile phone while driving a commercial vehicle. Using a hand-held phone is allowed only when needed to contact law enforcement or emergency services.
concepts.tip: Hands on the wheel. Pull over to make calls.

source.org: 49 CFR 392.80 and 392.82 (FMCSA)

concepts.definition: Driving a commercial motor vehicle with a BAC of 0.04% or more is illegal. Any detectable alcohol below 0.04% puts you out of service for 24 hours.
concepts.tip: Commercial limit is 0.04%, and any alcohol means 24 hours off.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 1

concepts.definition: A first offense (such as driving a CMV at 0.04% BAC or more, or refusing an alcohol test) means losing the CDL for at least 1 year, or at least 3 years if hauling placarded hazardous materials. A second offense means losing it for life.
concepts.tip: 1 year, 3 with hazmat, life for a second offense.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 1

concepts.definition: Sleep is the only cure for being tired. Warning signs include heavy eyes, constant yawning, drifting between lanes, and not remembering the last few miles. Pull off in a safe place and sleep or nap.
concepts.tip: Coffee is not sleep.

points: It is illegal to drive a CMV with a BAC of 0.04% or more.
Any detectable alcohol under 0.04% means 24 hours out of service.
Only time sobers you up. Coffee and fresh air do not.
No texting or hand-held phone use while driving a CMV, except to call emergency services.
When confronted by an aggressive driver, get out of the way and avoid eye contact.
If you are sleepy, get off the road and sleep.

summary: This chapter covers driving when you cannot see well or when weather makes the vehicle and road act differently: at night, in fog, in winter, and in very hot weather. In each case you need to slow down and check your vehicle more carefully.

At night, people see less sharply and are blinded by glare. Low beams let you see only about 250 feet ahead, so drive slowly enough to stop within your headlight range. Dim your lights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle or one you are following. In fog, the best choice is to pull off and wait. If you must drive, slow down before you enter it, use low beams and fog lights, and avoid passing.

In winter, check coolant, defrosters, wipers, tires, and chains, and watch for black ice, which makes the road look only wet. Bridges freeze before the road. After deep water, keep light pressure on the brakes to dry them. In very hot weather, check tires every 2 hours or 100 miles, never let air out of hot tires, and never remove the radiator cap until the system has cooled.

concepts.definition: Dim your high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and when following another vehicle within 500 feet. Use high beams when it is safe and legal.
concepts.tip: 500 feet, coming or going.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: Pull off to a rest area or truck stop if you can. If you must drive, slow down before entering the fog, use low beams and fog lights, turn on four-way flashers, and avoid passing.
concepts.tip: Low beams cut through fog. High beams bounce back.

concepts.definition: A thin layer of ice clear enough to see the road through it, so the road looks wet. Watch for it any time the temperature is below freezing and the road looks wet.
concepts.tip: Freezing and wet-looking means black ice.

concepts.definition: Water can make brakes weak, uneven, or grabby. After deep water, keep light pressure on the brakes for a short distance to dry them, then make a test stop when it is safe.
concepts.tip: Light pressure dries them, then test.

concepts.definition: Inspect tires every 2 hours or every 100 miles in very hot weather. Pressure rises with heat, so do not let air out. If a tire is too hot to touch, stay stopped until it cools.
concepts.tip: Hot tire: wait, do not deflate.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: Never remove the radiator cap or any part of the pressurized cooling system until it has cooled. Steam and boiling water can spray out and cause severe burns.
concepts.tip: If you cannot touch the cap bare-handed, leave it closed.

points: Dim your lights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle or a vehicle you follow.
Drive slowly enough to stop within the range of your headlights.
In fog, use low beams and fog lights, and avoid passing.
Bridges freeze before the road.
Never let air out of hot tires.
Never remove the radiator cap until the system has cooled.

summary: This chapter covers two places where a heavy vehicle has little room for error: railroad-highway crossings and long, steep grades. At a crossing, a train cannot stop for you. On a downgrade, gravity keeps pushing your speed up.

Approach every crossing expecting a train. Passive crossings have only signs and markings, so the decision is yours. Active crossings have flashing lights, bells, or gates. Do not race a train, do not rely only on signals, and do not shift gears on the tracks. A typical tractor-trailer needs at least 14 seconds to clear a single track and more than 15 seconds for a double track. If you get stuck, get out and away from the tracks, then call the emergency number posted at the crossing or 911.

Before a long downgrade, choose a safe speed for your weight, the grade, the road, and the weather, and shift to a low gear before you start down. Engine braking is your main speed control. Too much braking makes brakes fade from heat. Use the proper method: when you reach your safe speed, brake until you are about 5 mph below it, release, and repeat. Know where the escape ramps are.

concepts.definition: A passive crossing has no traffic control device, only signs and markings, so you decide whether it is safe. An active crossing has flashing red lights, with or without bells, and sometimes gates.
concepts.tip: Passive means the decision is all yours.

concepts.definition: Plan on a typical tractor-trailer taking 14 seconds or more to get across one set of tracks, and over 15 seconds when there are two sets. Never start across unless you can get all the way over.
concepts.tip: 14 seconds for one track, more for two.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks. Then use the emergency number posted at the crossing or call 911, and give the location and DOT number if posted.
concepts.tip: People first, truck second.

concepts.definition: Loss of braking power when brakes get too hot from overuse. You must press harder and harder for the same effect, until they may not slow you at all. Brakes out of adjustment make fade worse.
concepts.tip: Hot brakes are weak brakes.

concepts.definition: In the right low gear, when you reach your safe speed, brake hard enough to feel a definite slowdown. At about 5 mph below safe speed, release. The application lasts about 3 seconds. Repeat when you are back at safe speed.
concepts.tip: Safe speed, brake down 5 mph, release, repeat.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: A long bed of loose, soft material, sometimes going uphill, built to stop a runaway vehicle. Signs show where they are. If your brakes fail on a downgrade, use one.
concepts.tip: Know where the ramps are before you need one.

points: Do not shift gears while crossing railroad tracks.
A typical tractor-trailer needs at least 14 seconds to clear one track.
If you are stuck on the tracks, get out and away first, then call.
Shift to a low gear before you start down a grade.
Engine braking is the main way to control downhill speed.
Brake to about 5 mph below your safe speed, then release.

summary: This chapter covers what to do when something goes wrong suddenly: another vehicle in your path, a brake or tire failure, a skid, a crash, or a fire. Good habits help prevent emergencies, but when one happens, your chances depend on how well you act.

You can usually turn to miss an obstacle faster than you can stop. Keep both hands on the wheel, do not brake while turning, and be ready to countersteer. If an oncoming driver drifts into your lane, a move to the right is usually best. For emergency stops, use controlled braking or stab braking instead of jamming on the brakes. If a tire blows, hold the wheel firmly and stay off the brake until you slow down.

ABS keeps wheels from locking so you can steer, but it does not always shorten stopping distance. Most skids come from driving too fast for conditions. At a crash, protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured. For a fire, pull off in an open area, keep van doors closed for a cargo fire, and aim the extinguisher at the base of the fire from upwind.

concepts.definition: Turning around an obstacle is usually faster than stopping. Do not brake while turning, turn only as much as needed, and countersteer once you are past the obstacle.
concepts.tip: Steer and countersteer are one move.

concepts.definition: Controlled braking: brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels. Stab braking: brake fully, release when the wheels lock, and reapply when they roll again.
concepts.tip: Never just jam the pedal and hold it.

concepts.definition: Signs are a loud bang, heavy vibration, or heavy steering. Hold the wheel firmly, stay off the brake until the vehicle slows, then brake gently, pull off, and check all tires.
concepts.tip: Grip the wheel, not the brake.

concepts.definition: A computer system that keeps wheels from locking during hard braking so you can keep steering. It does not always shorten stopping distance, and if it fails you still have normal brakes.
concepts.tip: ABS is for control, not a shorter stop.

concepts.definition: For a drive-wheel braking skid, stop braking, steer quickly where you want to go, then countersteer. For a front-wheel skid, stop turning and braking so hard and let the vehicle slow down.
concepts.tip: Release the brake first in a skid.

concepts.definition: Pull off in an open area away from buildings and fuel, and call for help. Keep van doors shut for a cargo fire. Stand upwind, stay back, and aim at the base of the fire. Do not use water on electrical or gasoline fires.
concepts.tip: Upwind, at the base, doors closed.

points: You can usually turn to miss an obstacle faster than you can stop.
If an oncoming driver drifts into your lane, steer right.
After a blowout, hold the wheel firmly and stay off the brake.
ABS helps you steer, but it does not always shorten stopping distance.
At a crash: protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured.
Aim the extinguisher at the base of the fire.

summary: This chapter covers the driver's duty to haul cargo safely, even when someone else loaded it. Loose or poorly balanced cargo can fall off, shift in a quick stop, overload the vehicle, or make it hard to steer.

Check the cargo during your pre-trip inspection, again within the first 50 miles, and then every 3 hours or 150 miles and after every break. Know the weight terms: gross vehicle weight is what the vehicle and load actually weigh, and the rating is the maximum the manufacturer allows. Keep the load low with the heaviest items under the lightest, and balance it so the steering and drive axles each carry enough weight.

Use blocking, bracing, and tiedowns to stop cargo from moving. Use at least one tiedown for each 10 feet of cargo and never fewer than two. Cover open loads to protect people from spills and the cargo from weather. You cannot inspect a sealed load, but you must still make sure you are within gross and axle weight limits.

concepts.definition: Inspect cargo and securing devices within the first 50 miles of a trip, then after every 3 hours or 150 miles of driving, and after every break.
concepts.tip: 50 miles first, then 3 hours or 150 miles.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Sections 2 and 3

concepts.definition: Gross Vehicle Weight (GVW) is the actual total weight of a single vehicle and its load. Gross Vehicle Weight Rating (GVWR) is the maximum GVW set by the manufacturer. GCW and GCWR mean the same for combinations.
concepts.tip: The R stands for the maker's Rating (the limit).

concepts.definition: How high the weight sits. A high center of gravity makes rollover more likely, especially in curves or a swerve. Keep cargo low, with the heaviest items under the lightest.
concepts.tip: Heavy on the bottom, light on top.

concepts.definition: Too much weight on the steering axle makes steering hard. Too little makes the front too light to steer safely. Too little weight on the drive axles gives poor traction.
concepts.tip: Each axle needs its fair share.

concepts.definition: Use at least one tiedown for each 10 feet of cargo, and at least two no matter how small the cargo. The total working load limit must be at least half the cargo's weight.
concepts.tip: One per 10 feet, never fewer than two.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 3

points: Re-check cargo within the first 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles.
Use at least one tiedown per 10 feet of cargo, and at least two.
Put the heaviest cargo low, under the lightest cargo.
Too little weight on the front axle makes steering unsafe.
You cannot inspect a sealed load, but you must stay within weight limits.

summary: This chapter covers what every commercial driver must know about hazardous materials, even without the hazardous materials endorsement. Hazardous materials are products that pose a risk to health, safety, and property during transport, such as explosives, gases, flammable liquids, poisons, and corrosives.

The rules exist to contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment. Shippers describe the materials on shipping papers and put diamond-shaped labels on packages. Drivers must keep hazardous materials shipping papers where responders can find them: in a pouch on the driver's door, in clear view within reach while driving, or on the driver's seat when out of the vehicle.

Placards are diamond-shaped signs on the outside of the vehicle. A placarded vehicle needs at least four identical placards, on the front, rear, and both sides. If a vehicle requires placards, you may drive it only with the hazardous materials endorsement. Four-digit identification numbers, shown after UN or NA, help first responders identify the material.

concepts.definition: The rules have three goals: contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment.
concepts.tip: Contain, communicate, ensure safety.

concepts.definition: You may carry some hazardous materials without placards. But if the vehicle requires placards, you must have the hazardous materials endorsement on your CDL to drive it.
concepts.tip: Placards on the truck means the endorsement on the license.

concepts.definition: Diamond-shaped signs on the outside of the vehicle that show the hazard class of the cargo. A placarded vehicle needs at least four identical placards, front, rear, and both sides, each at least 10 3/4 inches square.
concepts.tip: Four sides, four placards.

source.org: New York State DMV Commercial Driver's Manual (CDL-10), Section 2

concepts.definition: Hazardous materials shipping papers must be marked or kept on top of other papers, and kept in a door pouch, in clear view within reach while driving, or on the driver's seat when you are out of the vehicle.
concepts.tip: Out of the cab, papers on the seat.

concepts.definition: A four-digit code, shown after the letters UN or NA, that first responders use to identify hazardous materials. The Emergency Response Guidebook lists them.
concepts.tip: Four digits after UN or NA.

points: A vehicle that requires placards needs a driver with the hazardous materials endorsement.
A placarded vehicle needs at least four identical placards.
Keep hazmat shipping papers in the door pouch, within reach, or on the seat when you are out.
The rules aim to contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment.
